## Joanna Baillie
Scottish poet and playwright Joanna Baillie (1762–1851) was so admired in her lifetime that her plays were compared to Shakespeare’s. Her most famous work was a set of comedies and tragedies called _Plays on the Passions_ (1798–1812). Baillie was interested in the inner workings of people’s minds, and the way that they could be driven to carry out terrible actions by feelings such as jealousy or pride. Each play from _Plays on the Passions_ explores a different state of mind, such as fear, love or hatred. _De Monfort_ (1821) features a man who plots to kill his childhood rival. Baillie’s uncles were the famous physicians William and John Hunter. Their work on human anatomy fascinated Baillie throughout her life, and inspired her to write about diseases of the body and mind.
​​​​​​​Baillie wrote 27 plays, as well as many poems. She supported anti-slavery campaigns and gave half of all her earnings to charity. Although she is not well-known today, Baillie’s focus on emotion in her plays helped spark the Romantic movement in literature, and influenced poets such as William Wordsworth and Lord Byron.

## Samuel Beckett
Samuel Beckett (1906–89) was an Irish playwright. He is known for his “tragi-comic” plays that explore hope, despair and the human instinct to survive. His plays tackle serious subjects in ways that are sometimes humorous, sometimes frightening. In his most famous play, _Waiting for Godot_(1953), two characters Vladimir (Didi) and Estragon (Gogo) wait together for the arrival of “Godot”, who is never introduced. The play has become so well-known that the English expression “to wait for Godot” has come to mean waiting for something to happen that never will. In another play, _Happy Days_ (1961), a woman talks cheerfully to her husband while she is buried up to her waist in the ground. These bizarre situations earned Beckett’s plays the label “theatre of the absurd”.
Later in Beckett’s life, his work became minimalistic: stripped to its essentials. His plays featured fewer parts and lines and even simpler staging. One, _Breath_ (1969), is just 35 seconds long. His 1972 play, _Not I_, features only a speaking mouth; the rest of the stage is in darkness. Beckett’s experimental writing had a huge influence on the playwrights, poets, film-makers and novelists of the 20th century. In 1969, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

## Aphra Behn
British playwright Aphra Behn (1640–89) was probably the first woman to earn a living by writing. Aged 26, Benn worked as a spy for the court of Charles II. But she did not earn enough money, so she soon turned to writing to make a living instead. Her first successful play was _The Rover_ (1681), a comedy about a group of men on holiday in Italy. Most of Behn’s plays were comedies, and she wrote about relationships in a daring and controversial way. Some, such as _The Emperor of the Moon_ (1687), were a type of comedy called farce, which creates humour by exaggerating situations.
​​​​​​​
Behn was inspired by a popular type of Italian comedy called _Commedia dell'arte_. With its easily recognizable characters and improvised scenes, it was a little like modern pantomime. Behn also wrote fiction. Her novel _Oroonoko_ (1688), about a young man sold into slavery in South America, was one of the first English novels. During Behn’s lifetime it was unusual for a woman to be a professional writer, and she used her celebrity to speak out for women’s rights. When she died, she was buried in Westminster Abbey.

## Bertolt Brecht
Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) was an influential German poet and playwright. He is famous for plays such as _The Threepenny Opera_ (1928), _The Caucasian Chalk Circle_ (1948) and _Mother Courage_(1956) which follows the story of a woman travelling across Europe during the Thirty Years' War (1618–48). Brecht also worked as a theatre director and critic, and his ideas were influential. He thought that theatre should reflect society and make us question the way that it is run, especially in the period after World War II. He wanted an audience to form opinions about what they were seeing in the play, rather than just be entertained. This style of theatre became known as epic theatre. Brecht’s plays were typically performed with simple staging, using only one or two props. Actors would sometimes "break out" of the play to address the audience directly.
Brecht was a communist whose experience of living through both world wars strongly influenced his writing. When Hitler came to power in the 1930s, Brecht left Germany and went to the USA. After World War II, he returned and set up a theatre called the Berliner Ensemble. By the time he died in 1956, Brecht had become known as one of Europe’s leading playwrights.

## Anton Chekhov
Anton Chekhov (1860–1904) was a Russian playwright and one of the greatest short story writers of his time. Chekhov began writing when he was a student to earn his tuition fees and support his family. He worked as a doctor, as well as a writer, for most of his life. He is best known for four major plays: _The Seagull_ (1895), _Uncle Vanya_ (1897), _Three Sisters_ (1901) and _The Cherry Orchard_ (1904). Instead of having action-packed storylines, Chekhov made his characters’ inner lives—their thoughts and emotions—the focus of his plays. This new way of writing plays would make him an influential figure in drama into the next century and beyond.
When his play _The Seagull_ was first performed at the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898, it was a sensation, because it was the first time a play had represented everyday life onstage rather than feature more dramatic events. The play follows the romantic and artistic lives of four people living in the Russian countryside. Anton Chekhov died of tuberculosis at the age of just 44.

## Caryl Churchill
Caryl Churchill (born 1938) is a British playwright known for plays such as _Top Girls_ (1982) and _The Skriker_ (1993). Churchill is one of the major feminist playwrights of the late 20th century. Her work reflected the growing movement of feminism that was happening in Britain at the time she began writing, the 1960s. In the 1970s she was part of a group of women playwrights called Monstrous Regiment that aimed to “put _real_ women on the stage”. Churchill’s plays usually look at an important political issue from a personal point of view. Her first stage play, _Owners_ (1972), was about a greedy landlady who wants to evict a young couple from a property she owns.
​​​​​​​
Churchill’s most famous play _Top Girls_(1982) follows Marlene, a successful businesswoman, and her sister Joyce, whose life as a single mother is more difficult. When writing the play, Churchill wanted her audience to see how women at the time were facing difficult choices in order to become “successful”. Churchill’s recent plays are written in an experimental style. Her 2012 play _Love and Information_ features more than 100 characters, has very few stage directions, and the scenes can be played in any order.

## Shelagh Delaney
Shelagh Delaney (1938–2011) was a British playwright best known for her 1958 play, _A Taste of Honey_. It follows the story of a single mother, Helen, and her pregnant teenage daughter Jo. Delaney’s first play, it was one of the earliest examples of a new type of writing in the 1950s and 60s called “kitchen sink” drama, which focused on people’s everyday lives, often at home. Delaney was one of the first British playwrights to write about working-class, female and gay characters. She was also one of the few women playwrights to have their voices heard in British theatre at the time. Following the success of _A Taste of Honey,_ which was made into a major film, Delaney wrote more plays for the stage, radio and television, but her first play remained her most successful.

## Goethe
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was a German poet, playwright, philosopher and politician. His writing and ideas shaped German culture during his lifetime and are influential to this day. His tragic play _Faust_ (written in two parts, the first published in 1808, the second in 1832), about a man who sells his soul to the Devil, is considered the greatest masterpiece of German literature. Goethe also wrote poetry (_Faust_ is written in verse) and novels. In his novel _The Sorrows of Young Werther_ (1774), he created the Romantic hero, an idea much copied by other writers across Europe. He became a leading figure in the _Sturm und Drang_ movement, a style of writing which frequently expressed extremes of emotion.
​​​​​​​
Goethe also developed a range of scientific interests, for example plant biology and the theory of colour (the way we see colours). He died of heart failure in 1832 in Weimar, where he spent much of his life.

## Lorraine Hansberry
Lorraine Hansberry (1930–65) was an American playwright. Her play _A Raisin in the Sun_ (1959) was the first by an African American to be produced on Broadway. It follows the story of a black family living in Chicago during the segregation era. It was inspired by Hansberry’s own childhood, where she and her family experienced racism. Throughout her life, Hansberry fought passionately for civil rights. In the early 1950s she protested against black people being evicted from their homes in Harlem, New York City. She wrote articles and essays arguing for women’s rights, and was a strong supporter of independence for colonial African countries. Hansberry died aged just 34. After her death, her collected writings and letters were made into a play about her life, called _To Be Young, Gifted and Black_ (1968).

## Lillian Hellman
Lillian Hellman (1905–84) was an American playwright. She wrote three major plays in the 1930s, when Fascism was spreading across Europe. Her first, _The Children’s Hour_ (1934), was about the way that slander (lies about someone) can ruin lives. Hellman’s plays encouraged her audience to consider moral dilemmas. _The Little Foxes_ (1939) is about a family who will go to any lengths to become rich. In _Watch on the Rhine_(1941) a man visiting the US from Europe kills a fascist man who threatens to put his friends’ lives in danger. The play carried the message that the US should join World War II and fight fascism.
​​​​​​​
Hellman’s plays were classed as melodrama, an intense, emotional type of play popular in the early 20th century which shows life to be more dramatic than it normally is. She was one of only a few American female playwrights to enjoy success in her time.

## Henrik Ibsen
Henrik Johan Ibsen (1828–1906) was a Norwegian playwright whose work was so influential that he is often known as “the father of modern drama”. Ibsen wrote plays about social issues—problems that affected many people in their day-to-day lives. His most famous play _A Doll’s House_(1879) is about the oppression of women. Like his later play, _Hedda Gabler_ (1890), it tells the story of a woman suffering in an unhappy marriage. Instead of showing a more dramatic version of everyday life onstage, Ibsen created situations that reflected real life. This new way of writing was known as realism: characters are presented as ordinary people who suffered from problems an audience would recognize. Ibsen used ordinary language that reflected the way people spoke.
​​​​​​​
Ibsen’s realism inspired a new generation of modern playwrights such as George Bernard Shaw, Arthur Miller and Eugene O’Neill. Ibsen grew up in Norway, but spent a large part of his life living in Italy and Germany, where he wrote his best known plays. By the time he returned to Norway in his 60s, he was a national hero. After Shakespeare, Ibsen’s plays are the most performed plays in the world.

## Eugène Ionesco
Eugène Ionesco (1909–94) was a Romanian-French playwright who was famous for "absurdist" plays. Ionesco’s early works were inspired by his experience of learning English at the age of 40. He found the example sentences in his phrasebook dull, and wrote a play about them to explore the idea that sometimes “making conversation” does not communicate very much at all. In his first play _The Bald Soprano_(1950), a couple making small talk suddenly realise with astonishment that they are husband and wife. The struggle to communicate was one of Ionesco’s favourite themes. It was the subject of several one-act (short) plays such as _The Chairs_ (1952) in which an elderly couple invite a huge crowd of guests to hear their life story, but nobody turns up. Ionesco's plays, along with those of Samuel Beckett and Jean Genet, are called the “theatre of the absurd”.
​​​​​​​
Ionesco’s best known play _Rhinoceros_ (1959) was his first play to become a success in English. In the play, people living in a French village are turned one by one into rhinoceroses. Many people saw it as symbolic of the way that Fascism had spread through Europe before World War II.

## Ben Jonson
Ben Jonson (1572–1637) was one of the major English poets and playwrights of the 17th century. He lived at the same time as William Shakespeare, who once acted in one of his plays. Most of Jonson’s plays were comedies, such as _Volpone_ (1605) and _The Alchemist_ (1610), and many were about greedy people coming up with schemes to become rich. Jonson wrote many “epigrams”—short, witty poems—and some of them were addressed to people he knew. One of his most famous poems, _On My First Sonne_(1616), was quite different to all the others. It was an elegy (a memorial poem) written in memory of his son, Ben, who had died aged seven.
​​​​​​​
Jonson’s work was very popular in his time. He was even supported by King James I, who sponsored him to write some of his plays and poetry. By the end of his life, Jonson was famous. Huge crowds attended his funeral in Westminster Abbey.

## Christopher Marlowe
Christopher Marlowe (1564–93) was an English poet and playwright. He was famous for the great tragedies he wrote during the late 16th century. His first play, _Tamburlaine the Great_ (1587), was an instant success when it was first performed in London. It tells the story of a shepherd, Timur, who becomes an emperor. It was remarkable because it was one of the first English plays to be written in blank verse, non-rhyming poetry that still follows a specific metre, or rhythmic pattern. After Marlowe used blank verse in his play, it became much more common for other playwrights to use it in theirs.
​​​​​​​
_Tamburlaine_ was the only one of Marlowe’s plays to be performed before he died. _Edward II_ (1593) tells the story of a king whose court decides to remove him from the throne. _Doctor Faustus_(written between 1589 and 1592) is about a scholar who sells his soul to the Devil in exchange for magical powers.
​​​​​​​Marlowe lived at the same time as Shakespeare, and he almost certainly worked with Shakespeare to write his three _Henry VI_ plays. Although Marlowe’s plays are still very famous today, little is known about his life. He was born in Canterbury. His father was a shoemaker, and, as a child, he won a scholarship to school and then Cambridge University. After he finished his studies, he worked for the government, probably as a spy. He was murdered in a fight aged just 29.

## Mustapha Matura
Mustapha Matura (1939–2019) was a Trinidadian playwright living in Britain. He was especially well known for writing plays about the experiences of Caribbean people, those living both in the UK and in the Caribbean. Born in Trinidad, Mustapha travelled to Britain as a young man in 1962 and then spent a year abroad in Rome, where he was inspired by his work on stage productions of Langston Hughes’ plays to write his own. His play _Black Pieces_(1970) was about Caribbean migrants exploring their identities as black people living in Britain. One of Matura’s most famous plays _Play Mas_ (1974) tells the story of the beginning of Trinidadian independence through the character of a tailor and his apprentice. In 1978, Matura co-founded the Black Theatre Co-operative to support black playwrights, actors and directors working in Britain.

## Arthur Miller
Arthur Miller (1915–2005) was an American playwright famous for his plays about the social issues facing ordinary Americans after World War II. Miller wrote most of his plays in a style called realism, which used natural language and depicted people in everyday settings. His plays often feature characters who have a difficult decision to make, or who are haunted by something they have done in the past. In _All My Sons_(1947) the main character is tormented by a decision he made during the war, while in _Death of a Salesman_ (1949) a man loses his job and watches his dream unravel. In _A View From the Bridge_ (1955) a man betrays his community by reporting illegal immigrants living there instead of helping them.

During the 1940s and 50s in the US, people suspected of being communists were being investigated by the US government and accused of being “Un-American”. This was a practice known as McCarthyism. In response, Miller wrote a play called _The Crucible_(1953) about a time in the 17th century when people who were accused of witchcraft were executed. He made a link between the Salem witchcraft trials and McCarthyism to alert his audience to what he regarded as comparable evils. For expressing these ideas, Miller was himself accused of being Un-American. Along with his marriage to the Hollywood actress Marilyn Monroe, it made him a celebrity at the time. Today, Miller is remembered as one of the major American playwrights of the 20th century. His plays have been adapted into films and continue to be performed all over the world.

## Molière
Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, better known by his pen name Molière (1622–73), was a major French writer of the 17th century. He is especially famous for comedies such as _Tartuffe_ (The Impostor, 1664), about a family who welcome a deceitful stranger into their home. Molière’s plays often made fun of pretentious people (those who pretend to be more important than they actually are). His plays were full of characters whose flaws, such as greed or jealousy, made their lives difficult and their stories dramatic. The plays broke the strict rules of theatre in France at the time: plays were to entertain; comedies had to end happily, while tragedies had to end with a death.
​​​​​​​
Molière’s play _The Misanthrope_ (1666) was controversial because it was neither a tragedy nor a comedy. It follows the story of a grumpy man named Alceste who refuses to live the life society expects of him.
​​​​​​​Theatre-goers loved his plays, but Molière was deeply unpopular with the Church. _Tartuffe_ was banned soon after it was first performed because Church officials saw it as an attack on religion. However, because Louis XIV supported Molière’s work, he was protected from criticism and so able to keep writing.
​​​​​​​When his plays were performed, Molière himself usually played the main character. He was on stage performing in his play _Le Malade Imaginaire_ (The Imaginary Invalid, 1673) when he went down with a coughing fit and died soon afterwards from tuberculosis. Molière is today considered one of the greatest writers in the French language.

## Lynn Nottage
Lynn Nottage (born 1964) is an American playwright known for her plays about modern life in the US, such as _Intimate Apparel_(2009) and _Sweat_(2015). Nottage’s plays tell stories about women, often those more usually overlooked by society. Her play _Ruined_ (2007) is about the difficult lives of women in a mining village in theDemocratic Republic of the Congo. It won the 2009 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. _Sweat,_ about a group of friends working in a factory, also won the Pulitzer Prize in 2017 (she is the only woman to have won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama twice).
​​​​​​​Nottage’s best-known play is _Intimate Apparel_. Set at the beginning of the 20th century, it follows the story of a woman who works as a factory seamstress, but who longs to run her own beauty parlour for African American women. The story was based on the life of Nottage’s own great-grandmother. Nottage is a professor of Playwriting at Columbia University, New York.

## Eugene O’Neill
Eugene O’Neill (1888–1953) was an American playwright whose tragic plays helped bring about a new way of writing. Influenced by European playwrights such as Anton Chekhov and August Strindberg, he introduced into American drama the idea that a play could focus on relationships between people, rather than involve dramatic action. He was also one of the first playwrights to use American slang in his plays.
O’Neill was the son of an actor, and spent his early years in the theatre touring with his father. As a young man, he worked as a sailor before becoming a playwright. His first full-length play _Beyond the Horizon_ (1920), a play about two brothers and their family, won him a Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
​​​​​​​
He went on to write some of his most famous plays during the 1930s and 40s, including _The Iceman Cometh_(1946) and _Mourning Becomes_ _Electra_ (1931). O’Neill’s greatest work, _Long Day’s Journey Into Night_ (1941), was performed only after his death. It follows four members of a family over a single day. O’Neill did not want it performed during his lifetime because the characters and events were based on those of his own family. In 1936 he became the first American playwright to receive the Nobel Prize for Literature.

## Harold Pinter
Harold Pinter (1930–2008) was a British playwright. He is especially well known for his tense plays about power and anxiety such as _The Birthday Party_ (1957) and _The Homecoming_ (1964). Pinter was born in London to Jewish parents. He began his career as an actor, and continued to act all his life alongside his writing. _The Birthday Party_ was Pinter’s second play. It was not a great success when it was first performed, but later became considered one of his finest plays. In the play, a man is terrorized by a pair of menacing strangers who arrive to throw him a party.
​​​​​​​
In 1960, Pinter made his name with _The Caretaker_ (1960), a play about two brothers who take in a homeless stranger. _The Homecoming_ explores the tense atmosphere between a family when they gather at their father’s house. Later plays such as _No Man's Land_ (1975) and _Betrayal_ (1978) became known as "memory plays" because the events of the play are drawn from the memory of one or more of the characters.
Pinter wrote in the naturalistic style that had become widespread by the 1950s, but he developed it to make it his own, introducing long pauses that filled his plays with suspense. Often Pinter’s characters speak a line which seems to be simple, but they are actually implying something else underneath. His style reflected the anxiety and unease in British society in the mid-20th century. The way he created an atmosphere in a play became so recognizable that the word “Pinteresque” was created to describe it. Pinter was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2005.

## Jean Racine
Jean Racine (1639–99) was a French playwright, the most famous writer of tragedy in French history. Nearly all Racine’s plays were set in the past. They either dealt with French history or retold classical Greek and Roman stories. He used these well known stories to comment on events in France at the time. His play _La Thébaide_(1664) was about identical twins, sons of the mythical Greek king Oedipus, competing to be the successor to the throne. His popular play _Andromaque_ (1667) told the story of Andromache, Hector’s widow, in the aftermath of the Trojan War.
​​​​​​​
In his only comedy _Les Plaideurs_(1668), Racine adapted ancient Greek playwright Aristophanes’ play _The Wasps_ and set it in France as a satire (comic impression) of the French legal system. His masterpiece _Phèdre_ (1677) was a retelling of Euripedes’ play _Hippolytus_, about a woman who falls in love with her stepson. After _Phèdre,_ Racine mostly retired from writing drama and went to work for the court of King Louis XIV.
Racine was a great master of a poetic metre called the alexandrine line, which he used to write his plays. It was a way of writing poetry in which each line had twelve syllables (beats). He made it so popular that from then on it became the main way of writing French tragedy.

## Friedrich Schiller
Friedrich Schiller (1759–1805) was a German playwright. Along with his friend Goethe, he started a movement called Weimar Classicism, which went on to influence German literature and culture for the next century. Also a poet, historian and philosopher, Schiller wrote many influential papers on personal freedom. As a young man, Schiller began his career in the army. During this time he wrote his first play _The Robbers_ (1781), about the rivalry between two brothers. When it was performed, it was a great success, but Schiller was expelled from the army for revealing his revolutionary politics. Schiller's 1785 poem _Ode to Joy_ was set by Ludwig van Beethoven in the fourth movement of his Ninth Symphony.
​​​​​​​
In 1794 Schiller became friends with Goethe. The friendship inspired him to write some of his greatest plays, such as _Mary Stuart_ (1800) and _William Tell_(1804), the story of a hero who leads peasants in a revolution. Schiller was famous during his lifetime. When his plays were performed, admirers would crowd the streets to try and catch a glimpse of him. Schiller died of tuberculosis at the age of just 46. His plays continue to be among the most popular performed in Germany.

## William Shakespeare
William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright known today as the greatest writer in the English language. His plays have been performed in theatres around the world for more than 400 years. Shakespeare wrote plays about history, as well as comedies, romances and tragedies. Their plots are often complex but contain real-life characters and deal with believable events. Shakespeare wrote 39 plays, as well as 154 sonnets (14-line poems).
We know only a little about Shakespeare's personal life (although we do know about certain things: his theatrical company and property dealings, for example). He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in Warwickshire, and began writing plays in 1592. He wrote them in a mixture of verse (lines of poetry) and prose (non-verse). Shakespeare invented a number of words which became part of the English language, and influences writers across the world to this day.
Shakespeare’s history plays, such as _Richard III_(1592)_,_ are full of murders, battles and evil scheming between the main characters. They tell the stories of the kings of England fighting wars against France. Among Shakespeare’s most famous comedies are _A Midsummer Night’s Dream_ (1595-6)and _Twelfth Night_ (1601), in which twins are separated by unfortunate events. Shakespeare’s romances are adventure stories that stir up great feelings of both joy and sadness. They include _A Winter’s Tale_(1611), in which a statue comes to life.
Shakespeare’s best-known plays are probably his great tragedies. Most of them are based on historical figures, each of whom meets a tragic end as a result of human failings such as greed or stupidity. _King Lear_ (1605-6) is about a king who dies of a broken heart, while _Romeo and Juliet_ (1595-6) tells the story of young lovers kept apart by their warring families. In _Hamlet_ (1600), a prince seeks revenge for his father’s death, but is killed by a poisoned sword.

## Wole Soyinka
Akinwande Oluwole Babatunde Soyinka (known as Wole Soyinka, born 1934) is a Nigerian playwright and poet. He is well known for writing about the politics and culture of Nigeria. His plays explore the difficulties of keeping a traditional way of life as the country became more modern. Born into a Yoruba family, Soyinka grew up in Nigeria before moving to Britain as a young man, where he wrote his first plays. One of them was _The Lion and the Jewel_ (1963), a comedy set in a Nigerian village with a darker story of violence underneath. Many of Soyinka’s plays are satires, plays that use humour to make fun of, or criticize something.
​​​​​​​
During the Nigerian Civil War, Soyinka was imprisoned for nearly two years when he wrote an article calling for a ceasefire (an end to the fighting).In 1986 Soyinka was the first African person to win the Nobel Prize for Literature. He works as a professor of literature and writing, teaching in universities all over the world.

## Tom Stoppard
Tom Stoppard (1937–2025) was a Czech-British playwright and screenwriter. Stoppard was born in Czechoslovakia (now Czechia) but fled from the Nazis with his family in 1939. He began his career as a journalist before moving to London in 1960, where he started writing plays. His first big success was _Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead_(1964–65), which retells the story of Shakespeare’s _Hamlet_ from the point of view of two court servants. In 1967 the play made him, at the age of 29, the youngest person ever to have a play performed at the National Theatre. _The Real Thing_(1982) is about a playwright, Henry, who writes plays about his relationship with his wife. Stoppard wove “real” scenes together with scenes from Henry’s plays to make his audience question reality. Stoppard also worked as a screenwriter—writing for television and film—and as a translator.

## The Glutton by A.K. Blakemore
_A subversive historical novel set during the French Revolution, inspired by a young peasant boy turned showman, said to have been tormented and driven to murder by an all-consuming appetite._
Take a step into the past, 1798 to be exact, where we find Tarare, The Glutton of Lyon in **A.K. Blakemore’s** latest novel, _**The Glutton**_. Nuns working in a Versailles hospital are watching over this man, who has a ravenous, insatiable appetite for, well … everything. And I mean everything. He will eat anything. Sister Perpetué has been asked to watch this sick patient overnight and has the opportunity to hear his wild story. As one of the seven deadly sins, she has been warned about this patient, to never leave him alone or believe his lies. But she can’t help but submit to her overwhelming curiosity.

## Path to Showmanship, Chaos and Murder
18th-century France is not a time I would like to live in. Conditions were hard, revolution was in the air and if you are not a member of the elite class, you are destined for a hard life. But Tarare loved his life, and started off innocent and blissfully unaware of how the “real world” worked. But when he and his mother are robbed, his stepfather decides enough is enough and tries to kill Tarare which sets him off on his new path. Moving from the life of a teenage peasant boy to one of showmanship, chaos and murder.
They say he ate a golden fork, but he’s also eaten rats, rusty nails, corks, and human flesh which all may be killing him from the inside. Tarare’s incredible and endless appetite is exploited by a band of misfits whom he teams up with for survival, but it all comes to a head when he sees their true colors. From there, he thinks joining the military will help him stay fed and quell his desires, but once his superiors find out his “talents” he is further exploited, this time putting him behind enemy lines where he is sent to deliver messages to the Prussian army. Ultimately, he finds himself in the hospital which is where this story begins and ends. But his life is a compilation of various horrors, all different but all related to one thing … that constant and bottomless hunger.

## Inspired by Historical Medical Records
What is amazing about this book is that The Glutton of Lyon previously existed only in medical records, and Blakemore has been able to craft a story that brings him to life — puts meat on his bones, if you will. This story is vivid but shows an unexpected side of the coin — the struggle that it must have been to be Tarare, the pressure and shame and torture that accompanied being The Glutton of Lyon.
This story is bizarre, dark, gruesome and violent with a sprinkle of sadness. Overall, it’s certainly not uplifting but the prose was incredible, so anyone who appreciates poetic and incredibly descriptive novels will love this. However, it is not for the faint of heart.
Tarare’s story is intermixed with Sister Perpetué’s thoughts on morality and the ethical nature of the story she is being told by her charge. This book makes you question things, makes you think about what you would do and ultimately had me feeling really horrible for Tarare, who was manipulated and exploited his entire life. It is beautiful, haunting and terrifying all at once, and it is certainly a book I will think about for some time.

## Joanna Baillie
Scottish poet and playwright Joanna Baillie (1762–1851) was so admired in her lifetime that her plays were compared to Shakespeare’s. Her most famous work was a set of comedies and tragedies called _Plays on the Passions_ (1798–1812). Baillie was interested in the inner workings of people’s minds, and the way that they could be driven to carry out terrible actions by feelings such as jealousy or pride. Each play from _Plays on the Passions_ explores a different state of mind, such as fear, love or hatred. _De Monfort_ (1821) features a man who plots to kill his childhood rival. Baillie’s uncles were the famous physicians William and John Hunter. Their work on human anatomy fascinated Baillie throughout her life, and inspired her to write about diseases of the body and mind.
​​​​​​​Baillie wrote 27 plays, as well as many poems. She supported anti-slavery campaigns and gave half of all her earnings to charity. Although she is not well-known today, Baillie’s focus on emotion in her plays helped spark the Romantic movement in literature, and influenced poets such as William Wordsworth and Lord Byron.

## Samuel Beckett
Samuel Beckett (1906–89) was an Irish playwright. He is known for his “tragi-comic” plays that explore hope, despair and the human instinct to survive. His plays tackle serious subjects in ways that are sometimes humorous, sometimes frightening. In his most famous play, _Waiting for Godot_(1953), two characters Vladimir (Didi) and Estragon (Gogo) wait together for the arrival of “Godot”, who is never introduced. The play has become so well-known that the English expression “to wait for Godot” has come to mean waiting for something to happen that never will. In another play, _Happy Days_ (1961), a woman talks cheerfully to her husband while she is buried up to her waist in the ground. These bizarre situations earned Beckett’s plays the label “theatre of the absurd”.
Later in Beckett’s life, his work became minimalistic: stripped to its essentials. His plays featured fewer parts and lines and even simpler staging. One, _Breath_ (1969), is just 35 seconds long. His 1972 play, _Not I_, features only a speaking mouth; the rest of the stage is in darkness. Beckett’s experimental writing had a huge influence on the playwrights, poets, film-makers and novelists of the 20th century. In 1969, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

## Aphra Behn
British playwright Aphra Behn (1640–89) was probably the first woman to earn a living by writing. Aged 26, Benn worked as a spy for the court of Charles II. But she did not earn enough money, so she soon turned to writing to make a living instead. Her first successful play was _The Rover_ (1681), a comedy about a group of men on holiday in Italy. Most of Behn’s plays were comedies, and she wrote about relationships in a daring and controversial way. Some, such as _The Emperor of the Moon_ (1687), were a type of comedy called farce, which creates humour by exaggerating situations.
​​​​​​​
Behn was inspired by a popular type of Italian comedy called _Commedia dell'arte_. With its easily recognizable characters and improvised scenes, it was a little like modern pantomime. Behn also wrote fiction. Her novel _Oroonoko_ (1688), about a young man sold into slavery in South America, was one of the first English novels. During Behn’s lifetime it was unusual for a woman to be a professional writer, and she used her celebrity to speak out for women’s rights. When she died, she was buried in Westminster Abbey.

## Bertolt Brecht
Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) was an influential German poet and playwright. He is famous for plays such as _The Threepenny Opera_ (1928), _The Caucasian Chalk Circle_ (1948) and _Mother Courage_(1956) which follows the story of a woman travelling across Europe during the Thirty Years' War (1618–48). Brecht also worked as a theatre director and critic, and his ideas were influential. He thought that theatre should reflect society and make us question the way that it is run, especially in the period after World War II. He wanted an audience to form opinions about what they were seeing in the play, rather than just be entertained. This style of theatre became known as epic theatre. Brecht’s plays were typically performed with simple staging, using only one or two props. Actors would sometimes "break out" of the play to address the audience directly.
Brecht was a communist whose experience of living through both world wars strongly influenced his writing. When Hitler came to power in the 1930s, Brecht left Germany and went to the USA. After World War II, he returned and set up a theatre called the Berliner Ensemble. By the time he died in 1956, Brecht had become known as one of Europe’s leading playwrights.

## Anton Chekhov
Anton Chekhov (1860–1904) was a Russian playwright and one of the greatest short story writers of his time. Chekhov began writing when he was a student to earn his tuition fees and support his family. He worked as a doctor, as well as a writer, for most of his life. He is best known for four major plays: _The Seagull_ (1895), _Uncle Vanya_ (1897), _Three Sisters_ (1901) and _The Cherry Orchard_ (1904). Instead of having action-packed storylines, Chekhov made his characters’ inner lives—their thoughts and emotions—the focus of his plays. This new way of writing plays would make him an influential figure in drama into the next century and beyond.
When his play _The Seagull_ was first performed at the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898, it was a sensation, because it was the first time a play had represented everyday life onstage rather than feature more dramatic events. The play follows the romantic and artistic lives of four people living in the Russian countryside. Anton Chekhov died of tuberculosis at the age of just 44.

## Caryl Churchill
Caryl Churchill (born 1938) is a British playwright known for plays such as _Top Girls_ (1982) and _The Skriker_ (1993). Churchill is one of the major feminist playwrights of the late 20th century. Her work reflected the growing movement of feminism that was happening in Britain at the time she began writing, the 1960s. In the 1970s she was part of a group of women playwrights called Monstrous Regiment that aimed to “put _real_ women on the stage”. Churchill’s plays usually look at an important political issue from a personal point of view. Her first stage play, _Owners_ (1972), was about a greedy landlady who wants to evict a young couple from a property she owns.
​​​​​​​
Churchill’s most famous play _Top Girls_(1982) follows Marlene, a successful businesswoman, and her sister Joyce, whose life as a single mother is more difficult. When writing the play, Churchill wanted her audience to see how women at the time were facing difficult choices in order to become “successful”. Churchill’s recent plays are written in an experimental style. Her 2012 play _Love and Information_ features more than 100 characters, has very few stage directions, and the scenes can be played in any order.

## Shelagh Delaney
Shelagh Delaney (1938–2011) was a British playwright best known for her 1958 play, _A Taste of Honey_. It follows the story of a single mother, Helen, and her pregnant teenage daughter Jo. Delaney’s first play, it was one of the earliest examples of a new type of writing in the 1950s and 60s called “kitchen sink” drama, which focused on people’s everyday lives, often at home. Delaney was one of the first British playwrights to write about working-class, female and gay characters. She was also one of the few women playwrights to have their voices heard in British theatre at the time. Following the success of _A Taste of Honey,_ which was made into a major film, Delaney wrote more plays for the stage, radio and television, but her first play remained her most successful.

## Goethe
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was a German poet, playwright, philosopher and politician. His writing and ideas shaped German culture during his lifetime and are influential to this day. His tragic play _Faust_ (written in two parts, the first published in 1808, the second in 1832), about a man who sells his soul to the Devil, is considered the greatest masterpiece of German literature. Goethe also wrote poetry (_Faust_ is written in verse) and novels. In his novel _The Sorrows of Young Werther_ (1774), he created the Romantic hero, an idea much copied by other writers across Europe. He became a leading figure in the _Sturm und Drang_ movement, a style of writing which frequently expressed extremes of emotion.
​​​​​​​
Goethe also developed a range of scientific interests, for example plant biology and the theory of colour (the way we see colours). He died of heart failure in 1832 in Weimar, where he spent much of his life.

## Lorraine Hansberry
Lorraine Hansberry (1930–65) was an American playwright. Her play _A Raisin in the Sun_ (1959) was the first by an African American to be produced on Broadway. It follows the story of a black family living in Chicago during the segregation era. It was inspired by Hansberry’s own childhood, where she and her family experienced racism. Throughout her life, Hansberry fought passionately for civil rights. In the early 1950s she protested against black people being evicted from their homes in Harlem, New York City. She wrote articles and essays arguing for women’s rights, and was a strong supporter of independence for colonial African countries. Hansberry died aged just 34. After her death, her collected writings and letters were made into a play about her life, called _To Be Young, Gifted and Black_ (1968).

## Lillian Hellman
Lillian Hellman (1905–84) was an American playwright. She wrote three major plays in the 1930s, when Fascism was spreading across Europe. Her first, _The Children’s Hour_ (1934), was about the way that slander (lies about someone) can ruin lives. Hellman’s plays encouraged her audience to consider moral dilemmas. _The Little Foxes_ (1939) is about a family who will go to any lengths to become rich. In _Watch on the Rhine_(1941) a man visiting the US from Europe kills a fascist man who threatens to put his friends’ lives in danger. The play carried the message that the US should join World War II and fight fascism.
​​​​​​​
Hellman’s plays were classed as melodrama, an intense, emotional type of play popular in the early 20th century which shows life to be more dramatic than it normally is. She was one of only a few American female playwrights to enjoy success in her time.

## Henrik Ibsen
Henrik Johan Ibsen (1828–1906) was a Norwegian playwright whose work was so influential that he is often known as “the father of modern drama”. Ibsen wrote plays about social issues—problems that affected many people in their day-to-day lives. His most famous play _A Doll’s House_(1879) is about the oppression of women. Like his later play, _Hedda Gabler_ (1890), it tells the story of a woman suffering in an unhappy marriage. Instead of showing a more dramatic version of everyday life onstage, Ibsen created situations that reflected real life. This new way of writing was known as realism: characters are presented as ordinary people who suffered from problems an audience would recognize. Ibsen used ordinary language that reflected the way people spoke.
​​​​​​​
Ibsen’s realism inspired a new generation of modern playwrights such as George Bernard Shaw, Arthur Miller and Eugene O’Neill. Ibsen grew up in Norway, but spent a large part of his life living in Italy and Germany, where he wrote his best known plays. By the time he returned to Norway in his 60s, he was a national hero. After Shakespeare, Ibsen’s plays are the most performed plays in the world.

## Eugène Ionesco
Eugène Ionesco (1909–94) was a Romanian-French playwright who was famous for "absurdist" plays. Ionesco’s early works were inspired by his experience of learning English at the age of 40. He found the example sentences in his phrasebook dull, and wrote a play about them to explore the idea that sometimes “making conversation” does not communicate very much at all. In his first play _The Bald Soprano_(1950), a couple making small talk suddenly realise with astonishment that they are husband and wife. The struggle to communicate was one of Ionesco’s favourite themes. It was the subject of several one-act (short) plays such as _The Chairs_ (1952) in which an elderly couple invite a huge crowd of guests to hear their life story, but nobody turns up. Ionesco's plays, along with those of Samuel Beckett and Jean Genet, are called the “theatre of the absurd”.
​​​​​​​
Ionesco’s best known play _Rhinoceros_ (1959) was his first play to become a success in English. In the play, people living in a French village are turned one by one into rhinoceroses. Many people saw it as symbolic of the way that Fascism had spread through Europe before World War II.

## Ben Jonson
Ben Jonson (1572–1637) was one of the major English poets and playwrights of the 17th century. He lived at the same time as William Shakespeare, who once acted in one of his plays. Most of Jonson’s plays were comedies, such as _Volpone_ (1605) and _The Alchemist_ (1610), and many were about greedy people coming up with schemes to become rich. Jonson wrote many “epigrams”—short, witty poems—and some of them were addressed to people he knew. One of his most famous poems, _On My First Sonne_(1616), was quite different to all the others. It was an elegy (a memorial poem) written in memory of his son, Ben, who had died aged seven.
​​​​​​​
Jonson’s work was very popular in his time. He was even supported by King James I, who sponsored him to write some of his plays and poetry. By the end of his life, Jonson was famous. Huge crowds attended his funeral in Westminster Abbey.

## Christopher Marlowe
Christopher Marlowe (1564–93) was an English poet and playwright. He was famous for the great tragedies he wrote during the late 16th century. His first play, _Tamburlaine the Great_ (1587), was an instant success when it was first performed in London. It tells the story of a shepherd, Timur, who becomes an emperor. It was remarkable because it was one of the first English plays to be written in blank verse, non-rhyming poetry that still follows a specific metre, or rhythmic pattern. After Marlowe used blank verse in his play, it became much more common for other playwrights to use it in theirs.
​​​​​​​
_Tamburlaine_ was the only one of Marlowe’s plays to be performed before he died. _Edward II_ (1593) tells the story of a king whose court decides to remove him from the throne. _Doctor Faustus_(written between 1589 and 1592) is about a scholar who sells his soul to the Devil in exchange for magical powers.
​​​​​​​Marlowe lived at the same time as Shakespeare, and he almost certainly worked with Shakespeare to write his three _Henry VI_ plays. Although Marlowe’s plays are still very famous today, little is known about his life. He was born in Canterbury. His father was a shoemaker, and, as a child, he won a scholarship to school and then Cambridge University. After he finished his studies, he worked for the government, probably as a spy. He was murdered in a fight aged just 29.

## Mustapha Matura
Mustapha Matura (1939–2019) was a Trinidadian playwright living in Britain. He was especially well known for writing plays about the experiences of Caribbean people, those living both in the UK and in the Caribbean. Born in Trinidad, Mustapha travelled to Britain as a young man in 1962 and then spent a year abroad in Rome, where he was inspired by his work on stage productions of Langston Hughes’ plays to write his own. His play _Black Pieces_(1970) was about Caribbean migrants exploring their identities as black people living in Britain. One of Matura’s most famous plays _Play Mas_ (1974) tells the story of the beginning of Trinidadian independence through the character of a tailor and his apprentice. In 1978, Matura co-founded the Black Theatre Co-operative to support black playwrights, actors and directors working in Britain.

Arthur Miller (1915–2005) was an American playwright famous for his plays about the social issues facing ordinary Americans after World War II. Miller wrote most of his plays in a style called realism, which used natural language and depicted people in everyday settings. His plays often feature characters who have a difficult decision to make, or who are haunted by something they have done in the past. In _All My Sons_(1947) the main character is tormented by a decision he made during the war, while in _Death of a Salesman_ (1949) a man loses his job and watches his dream unravel. In _A View From the Bridge_ (1955) a man betrays his community by reporting illegal immigrants living there instead of helping them.

## Molière
Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, better known by his pen name Molière (1622–73), was a major French writer of the 17th century. He is especially famous for comedies such as _Tartuffe_ (The Impostor, 1664), about a family who welcome a deceitful stranger into their home. Molière’s plays often made fun of pretentious people (those who pretend to be more important than they actually are). His plays were full of characters whose flaws, such as greed or jealousy, made their lives difficult and their stories dramatic. The plays broke the strict rules of theatre in France at the time: plays were to entertain; comedies had to end happily, while tragedies had to end with a death.
​​​​​​​
Molière’s play _The Misanthrope_ (1666) was controversial because it was neither a tragedy nor a comedy. It follows the story of a grumpy man named Alceste who refuses to live the life society expects of him.
​​​​​​​Theatre-goers loved his plays, but Molière was deeply unpopular with the Church. _Tartuffe_ was banned soon after it was first performed because Church officials saw it as an attack on religion. However, because Louis XIV supported Molière’s work, he was protected from criticism and so able to keep writing.
​​​​​​​When his plays were performed, Molière himself usually played the main character. He was on stage performing in his play _Le Malade Imaginaire_ (The Imaginary Invalid, 1673) when he went down with a coughing fit and died soon afterwards from tuberculosis. Molière is today considered one of the greatest writers in the French language.

## Lynn Nottage
Lynn Nottage (born 1964) is an American playwright known for her plays about modern life in the US, such as _Intimate Apparel_(2009) and _Sweat_(2015). Nottage’s plays tell stories about women, often those more usually overlooked by society. Her play _Ruined_ (2007) is about the difficult lives of women in a mining village in theDemocratic Republic of the Congo. It won the 2009 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. _Sweat,_ about a group of friends working in a factory, also won the Pulitzer Prize in 2017 (she is the only woman to have won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama twice).
​​​​​​​Nottage’s best-known play is _Intimate Apparel_. Set at the beginning of the 20th century, it follows the story of a woman who works as a factory seamstress, but who longs to run her own beauty parlour for African American women. The story was based on the life of Nottage’s own great-grandmother. Nottage is a professor of Playwriting at Columbia University, New York.

## Eugene O’Neill
Eugene O’Neill (1888–1953) was an American playwright whose tragic plays helped bring about a new way of writing. Influenced by European playwrights such as Anton Chekhov and August Strindberg, he introduced into American drama the idea that a play could focus on relationships between people, rather than involve dramatic action. He was also one of the first playwrights to use American slang in his plays.
O’Neill was the son of an actor, and spent his early years in the theatre touring with his father. As a young man, he worked as a sailor before becoming a playwright. His first full-length play _Beyond the Horizon_ (1920), a play about two brothers and their family, won him a Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
​​​​​​​
He went on to write some of his most famous plays during the 1930s and 40s, including _The Iceman Cometh_(1946) and _Mourning Becomes_ _Electra_ (1931). O’Neill’s greatest work, _Long Day’s Journey Into Night_ (1941), was performed only after his death. It follows four members of a family over a single day. O’Neill did not want it performed during his lifetime because the characters and events were based on those of his own family. In 1936 he became the first American playwright to receive the Nobel Prize for Literature.

## Harold Pinter
Harold Pinter (1930–2008) was a British playwright. He is especially well known for his tense plays about power and anxiety such as _The Birthday Party_ (1957) and _The Homecoming_ (1964). Pinter was born in London to Jewish parents. He began his career as an actor, and continued to act all his life alongside his writing. _The Birthday Party_ was Pinter’s second play. It was not a great success when it was first performed, but later became considered one of his finest plays. In the play, a man is terrorized by a pair of menacing strangers who arrive to throw him a party.
​​​​​​​
In 1960, Pinter made his name with _The Caretaker_ (1960), a play about two brothers who take in a homeless stranger. _The Homecoming_ explores the tense atmosphere between a family when they gather at their father’s house. Later plays such as _No Man's Land_ (1975) and _Betrayal_ (1978) became known as "memory plays" because the events of the play are drawn from the memory of one or more of the characters.
Pinter wrote in the naturalistic style that had become widespread by the 1950s, but he developed it to make it his own, introducing long pauses that filled his plays with suspense. Often Pinter’s characters speak a line which seems to be simple, but they are actually implying something else underneath. His style reflected the anxiety and unease in British society in the mid-20th century. The way he created an atmosphere in a play became so recognizable that the word “Pinteresque” was created to describe it. Pinter was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2005.

## Jean Racine
Jean Racine (1639–99) was a French playwright, the most famous writer of tragedy in French history. Nearly all Racine’s plays were set in the past. They either dealt with French history or retold classical Greek and Roman stories. He used these well known stories to comment on events in France at the time. His play _La Thébaide_(1664) was about identical twins, sons of the mythical Greek king Oedipus, competing to be the successor to the throne. His popular play _Andromaque_ (1667) told the story of Andromache, Hector’s widow, in the aftermath of the Trojan War.
​​​​​​​
In his only comedy _Les Plaideurs_(1668), Racine adapted ancient Greek playwright Aristophanes’ play _The Wasps_ and set it in France as a satire (comic impression) of the French legal system. His masterpiece _Phèdre_ (1677) was a retelling of Euripedes’ play _Hippolytus_, about a woman who falls in love with her stepson. After _Phèdre,_ Racine mostly retired from writing drama and went to work for the court of King Louis XIV.
Racine was a great master of a poetic metre called the alexandrine line, which he used to write his plays. It was a way of writing poetry in which each line had twelve syllables (beats). He made it so popular that from then on it became the main way of writing French tragedy.

## Friedrich Schiller
Friedrich Schiller (1759–1805) was a German playwright. Along with his friend Goethe, he started a movement called Weimar Classicism, which went on to influence German literature and culture for the next century. Also a poet, historian and philosopher, Schiller wrote many influential papers on personal freedom. As a young man, Schiller began his career in the army. During this time he wrote his first play _The Robbers_ (1781), about the rivalry between two brothers. When it was performed, it was a great success, but Schiller was expelled from the army for revealing his revolutionary politics. Schiller's 1785 poem _Ode to Joy_ was set by Ludwig van Beethoven in the fourth movement of his Ninth Symphony.
​​​​​​​
In 1794 Schiller became friends with Goethe. The friendship inspired him to write some of his greatest plays, such as _Mary Stuart_ (1800) and _William Tell_(1804), the story of a hero who leads peasants in a revolution. Schiller was famous during his lifetime. When his plays were performed, admirers would crowd the streets to try and catch a glimpse of him. Schiller died of tuberculosis at the age of just 46. His plays continue to be among the most popular performed in Germany.

## William Shakespeare
William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright known today as the greatest writer in the English language. His plays have been performed in theatres around the world for more than 400 years. Shakespeare wrote plays about history, as well as comedies, romances and tragedies. Their plots are often complex but contain real-life characters and deal with believable events. Shakespeare wrote 39 plays, as well as 154 sonnets (14-line poems).
We know only a little about Shakespeare's personal life (although we do know about certain things: his theatrical company and property dealings, for example). He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in Warwickshire, and began writing plays in 1592. He wrote them in a mixture of verse (lines of poetry) and prose (non-verse). Shakespeare invented a number of words which became part of the English language, and influences writers across the world to this day.
Shakespeare’s history plays, such as _Richard III_(1592)_,_ are full of murders, battles and evil scheming between the main characters. They tell the stories of the kings of England fighting wars against France. Among Shakespeare’s most famous comedies are _A Midsummer Night’s Dream_ (1595-6)and _Twelfth Night_ (1601), in which twins are separated by unfortunate events. Shakespeare’s romances are adventure stories that stir up great feelings of both joy and sadness. They include _A Winter’s Tale_(1611), in which a statue comes to life.
Shakespeare’s best-known plays are probably his great tragedies. Most of them are based on historical figures, each of whom meets a tragic end as a result of human failings such as greed or stupidity. _King Lear_ (1605-6) is about a king who dies of a broken heart, while _Romeo and Juliet_ (1595-6) tells the story of young lovers kept apart by their warring families. In _Hamlet_ (1600), a prince seeks revenge for his father’s death, but is killed by a poisoned sword.
texts.24:
## Wole Soyinka
Akinwande Oluwole Babatunde Soyinka (known as Wole Soyinka, born 1934) is a Nigerian playwright and poet. He is well known for writing about the politics and culture of Nigeria. His plays explore the difficulties of keeping a traditional way of life as the country became more modern. Born into a Yoruba family, Soyinka grew up in Nigeria before moving to Britain as a young man, where he wrote his first plays. One of them was _The Lion and the Jewel_ (1963), a comedy set in a Nigerian village with a darker story of violence underneath. Many of Soyinka’s plays are satires, plays that use humour to make fun of, or criticize something.
​​​​​​​
During the Nigerian Civil War, Soyinka was imprisoned for nearly two years when he wrote an article calling for a ceasefire (an end to the fighting).In 1986 Soyinka was the first African person to win the Nobel Prize for Literature. He works as a professor of literature and writing, teaching in universities all over the world.

## Tom Stoppard
Tom Stoppard (1937–2025) was a Czech-British playwright and screenwriter. Stoppard was born in Czechoslovakia (now Czechia) but fled from the Nazis with his family in 1939. He began his career as a journalist before moving to London in 1960, where he started writing plays. His first big success was _Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead_(1964–65), which retells the story of Shakespeare’s _Hamlet_ from the point of view of two court servants. In 1967 the play made him, at the age of 29, the youngest person ever to have a play performed at the National Theatre. _The Real Thing_(1982) is about a playwright, Henry, who writes plays about his relationship with his wife. Stoppard wove “real” scenes together with scenes from Henry’s plays to make his audience question reality. Stoppard also worked as a screenwriter—writing for television and film—and as a translator.

## The Glutton by A.K. Blakemore
_A subversive historical novel set during the French Revolution, inspired by a young peasant boy turned showman, said to have been tormented and driven to murder by an all-consuming appetite._
Take a step into the past, 1798 to be exact, where we find Tarare, The Glutton of Lyon in **A.K. Blakemore’s** latest novel, _**The Glutton**_. Nuns working in a Versailles hospital are watching over this man, who has a ravenous, insatiable appetite for, well … everything. And I mean everything. He will eat anything. Sister Perpetué has been asked to watch this sick patient overnight and has the opportunity to hear his wild story. As one of the seven deadly sins, she has been warned about this patient, to never leave him alone or believe his lies. But she can’t help but submit to her overwhelming curiosity.
texts.1:
## Path to Showmanship, Chaos and Murder
18th-century France is not a time I would like to live in. Conditions were hard, revolution was in the air and if you are not a member of the elite class, you are destined for a hard life. But Tarare loved his life, and started off innocent and blissfully unaware of how the “real world” worked. But when he and his mother are robbed, his stepfather decides enough is enough and tries to kill Tarare which sets him off on his new path. Moving from the life of a teenage peasant boy to one of showmanship, chaos and murder.
They say he ate a golden fork, but he’s also eaten rats, rusty nails, corks, and human flesh which all may be killing him from the inside. Tarare’s incredible and endless appetite is exploited by a band of misfits whom he teams up with for survival, but it all comes to a head when he sees their true colors. From there, he thinks joining the military will help him stay fed and quell his desires, but once his superiors find out his “talents” he is further exploited, this time putting him behind enemy lines where he is sent to deliver messages to the Prussian army. Ultimately, he finds himself in the hospital which is where this story begins and ends. But his life is a compilation of various horrors, all different but all related to one thing … that constant and bottomless hunger.
texts.2:
## Inspired by Historical Medical Records
What is amazing about this book is that The Glutton of Lyon previously existed only in medical records, and Blakemore has been able to craft a story that brings him to life — puts meat on his bones, if you will. This story is vivid but shows an unexpected side of the coin — the struggle that it must have been to be Tarare, the pressure and shame and torture that accompanied being The Glutton of Lyon.
This story is bizarre, dark, gruesome and violent with a sprinkle of sadness. Overall, it’s certainly not uplifting but the prose was incredible, so anyone who appreciates poetic and incredibly descriptive novels will love this. However, it is not for the faint of heart.
Tarare’s story is intermixed with Sister Perpetué’s thoughts on morality and the ethical nature of the story she is being told by her charge. This book makes you question things, makes you think about what you would do and ultimately had me feeling really horrible for Tarare, who was manipulated and exploited his entire life. It is beautiful, haunting and terrifying all at once, and it is certainly a book I will think about for some time.
* * *
**About A.K. Blakemore:**
A.K. Blakemore is the author of two collections of poetry:_Humbert Summer_ and _Fondue_. She has also translated the work of Sichuanese poet Yu Yoyo. Her poetry and prose writing have been widely published and anthologized, appearing in _The_ _London Review of Books_,_Poetry_,_The Poetry Review_, and _The White Review_, among other publications. Her debut novel,_The Manningtree Witches_ won the Desmond Elliot Prize 2021. She lives in London, England.

# The Glutton
Written by A. K. BLAKEMORE
Review by Katherine Mezzacappa
France, 1798: A patient presents himself at a public hospital in a wretched, moribund condition, claiming to have swallowed a golden fork that tears at his insides. Blakemore’s novel is based on the true story of Tarare, a circus entertainer from near Lyon, capable of eating anything: dead rats, offal, live animals too – and in vast quantities. Unable to satisfy his gargantuan appetite, he ultimately transgresses the greatest of taboos. Sister Perpetué stands guard on the shackled Tarare overnight, under strict instructions not to leave him. She and her sisters have survived the Terror where other professed women have not, because no-one else will care for the sick as they do.
Sr. Perpetué is both fascinated and disgusted by this Hannibal Lecter of the revolutionary era. He is physically repellent, his belly grossly distended though his cheeks are concave. His teeth are rotten stumps, and he stinks. But now, dying of tuberculosis, he is also pitiful, despite what he has done. Indeed, Blakemore’s great achievement is to tell with empathy the story of what had once been a child ‘with a smile as blank and open as a hilltop.’ Tarare’s history unfolds in sustained flashbacks: his morbid appetite appears after an act of extreme violence; he falls in with a group of itinerant entertainers who exhibit him as a freak. He does not know what to do with the kindness a young prostitute offers him, so he clumsily drives her from him. Later, his extraordinary digestion leads to a brief, unsuccessful career as a spy.
This is a compelling but not always easy read (perhaps you too would need to look up ‘feculent’ and ‘atrabilious’), but it is utterly convincing. It is definitely not for the faint-hearted or the squeamish.

#### History of the Musical Stage


#### by John Kenrick
(Copyright 1996; revised 2020)
*   Harrigan & Hart  
*   The Mulligan Shows  
*   Forgotten Hits
**(The images below are thumbnails – click on them to see larger versions.)**

### Harrigan and Hart
**Tony Hart, Ned Harrigan and an unnamed assistant perform "The Mulligan Guard March.**
Some British sources credit London producer **George Edwardes** with creating the first musical comedies. He began using this phrase to describe his shows as of 1893, and most of his Gaiety Theater productions were little more than Gilbert and Sullivan-style operettas with chorines in shortened skirts. But someone on the other side of the "pond" beat him to it.
The form we know as **musical comedy** was actually born on Broadway in a series of shows starring **Edward (Ned) Harrigan** and **Tony Hart**. Produced between 1878 and 1884, with book and lyrics by Harrigan and music by his father in law **David Braham**, these musical comedies featured characters and situations taken from the everyday life of New York's lower classes -- minus any sign of showgirls. With these distinctly American book musicals, Harrigan, Hart and Braham laid a path that Broadway would follow profitably for more than a century to come.
Harrigan started out as a comedian in the variety halls of San Francisco. Hart was a stage-struck reform school escapee with a rare gift for comedy. They met the mid-1870s, and developed a routine that poked fun at New York's neighborhood militias. These local "guard" units were little more than uniformed drinking clubs sponsored by local politicians. Weekend parades usually became so beer-soaked that the stumbling participants looked ridiculous. In their variety act, Harrigan and Hart donned ill-fitting uniforms and staggered through an inept military drill while singing a merry march.
> _We shouldered arms  
>   
>  And marched  
>   
>  And marched away,  
>   
>  From Baxter Street  
>   
>  We marched to Avenue A.  
>   
>  With drums and fifes  
>   
>  How sweetly they did play  
>   
>  As we marched, marched, marched  
>   
>  In the Mulligan Guards._
Audiences loved the act, and the catchy "Mulligan Guard's March" was soon being sung all around the world. In the novel _Kim_, Rudyard Kipling notes that it was a favorite with British troops in India who replaced the names of New York streets with various Indian locales.

### The Mulligan Shows
When Harrigan and Hart reached New York, their "Mulligan Guard" act was such a sensation that it played the city's top variety theaters for more than a year. In order to capitalize on this acclaim, the team expanded the act into **_The Mulligan Guard Picnic_ (1878)**, a forty minute sketch that drew packed audiences into Broadway's Theatre Comique for a month -- a healthy commercial run for that time. This initiated a seven year series of full length musical farces. The versatile Harrigan performed, produced, and directed while writing the scripts and lyrics. The action was always set in the scruffiest wards of downtown Manhattan, with Harrigan playing politically ambitious Irish saloon owner "Dan Mulligan" and Hart winning praise as various characters, most notably the African American washerwoman "Rebecca Allup."
**_The Mulligan Guard Ball_ (1879)**, **_Cordelia's Aspirations_ (1883)** and the rest of the series proved extremely popular with New York's immigrant-based lower and middle classes, who loved seeing themselves depicted on stage. Powerful politicians made a point of showing up too, anxious to curry the favor of voters. Harrigan & Hart's plots focused on such real-life problems as interracial tensions, uneasy romances between members of different ethinicities, political corruption and gang violence, but these were always served up with enough clownish humor to keep audiences laughing. Since every class and ethnic group was treated as fair game (and often depicted with surprising sympathy), nobody took offense.
Harrigan's dialogue relied heavily on puns and ethnic dialects to win laughs. In _Squatter Sovereignty_ (1882), an Irish immigrant has the following exchange with his wife when he realizes a fish has been tied to his back as an April Fool's Day prank –
> **MICHAEL:** Be heavens, that's a _haddock_.  
>   
> **ELLEN:** 'Tis, and was hanging to a _sucker_.  
>   
> **MICHAEL:** You're only _codding_ me.  
>   
> **ELLEN:** What _eels_ you?  
>   
> **MICHAEL:** I've _smelt_ that before.

### The Mulligan Shows
**Program for _The Mulligan Guard Ball_ (1883). I discovered this tucked between the pages of a tattered Victorian novel -- you never know what might be hiding at your local flea market.**
Harrigan and Braham's songs were in the popular style of their day, with lots of sentiment mixed with street-smart humor set to simple, catchy melodies. The lyrics were redolent with slang, ethnic accents and imperfect grammar -- speech forms which had not been set to music before. New Yorkers adored these tunes, and every neighborhood in Manhattan rang with renditions of "Paddy Duffy's Cart" or **"The Babies on Our Block,"** which describes some aspects of Irish tenement life –
> _If you want for information  
>   
>  Or in need of merriment,  
>   
>  Come over with me socially  
>   
>  To Murphy's tenement.  
>   
>  He owns a row of houses  
>   
>  In the first ward, near the dock,  
>   
>  Where Ireland's represented  
>   
>  By the babies on our block.  
>   
>  There's the Phalens and the Whalens  
>   
>  From the sweet Dunochadee,  
>   
>  They are sitting on the railings  
>   
>  With their children on their knee,  
>   
>  All gossiping and talking  
>   
>  With their neighbors in a flock,  
>   
>  Singing "Little Sally Waters"  
>   
>  With the babies on our block.  
>   
>  "Oh, little Sally Waters,  
>   
>  Sitting in the sun,  
>   
>  A-crying and weeping for a young man;  
>   
>  Oh rise, Sally, rise,  
>   
>  Wipe your eye out with your frock";  
>   
>  That's sung by the babies  
>   
>  A-living on our block._  
>   
> **- Lyric transcribed from sheet music**
Since these songs were only peripherally connected to the plots of the shows, hits from previous Braham-Harrigan scores could be interpolated when things needed a lift. In particular, Harrigan and Hart often reprised their "Mulligan Guards March," to show-stopping effect.

### The Mulligan Shows
Over time, Harrigan's habit of hiring relatives alienated Hart, and the team split up in 1885. Hart went off on his own, but the crippling effects of advanced syphilis forced him off the stage the following year, and he died soon afterwards at age 36. Harrigan continued to produce and star in musicals until 1893. **George M. Cohan**'s jaunty song "H-A-double R-I-G-A-N spells Harrigan" was an affectionate tribute to this early giant of the American musical stage.
> **For more on Harrigan & Hart:**
*   **Kahn, E.J. _The Merry Partners: The Age and Stage of Harrigan and Hart._** (New York: Random House, 1955)  
*   **Moody, Richard. _Ned Harrigan - From Corlear's Hook to Herald Square._** (Chicago: Nelson Hall, 1980)

### Forgotten Hits
There were other troupes offering musical comedy in the 1870s and 80s. The Salisbury Troubadours brought their touring production of **_The Brook_ (1879)**to Broadway, where it lasted a then-profitable six weeks. Several sources claim that _The Brook_ contained the first seeds of modern musical comedy, but this is questionable. The plot involved two women and three men who go on a picnic via a short boat ride. Along with food, their picnic baskets produced the costumes and props for specialty numbers, turning the show into a vaudeville-style procession of acts. The songs were recycled from various sources. By the time this mishmash reached New York, Harrigan and Hart were already a going concern.
During the 1880s, Broadway musicals became more numerous and profitable than ever. Aside from the imported works of Gilbert & Sullivan (discussed elsewhere in these essays), most of the hits from this decade are forgotten today. However, at least one American musical from this period remained popular well into the next century.
**Francis Wilson (seated) as the cowardly thief Cadeaux, and William S. Daboll as his daring partner Ravennes are plotting a kidnapping in _Erminie_ (1886).**
**_Erminie_ (London 1885, NY 1886)** was the tale of two thieves who kidnap a young bride in hopes of a ransom, inadvertently liberating the girl from a marriage she dreads. This lighthearted silliness ran for over 500 performances in London, and was revived so often on Broadway that it racked up more than 1,200 performances there by 1900. As the timorous thief Cadeaux, **Francis Wilson** achieved lasting stardom. Unlike most of the stage clowns of his time, Wilson did not rely on physical mugging to win laughs --
> "Wilson's comedy and farce were rooted in his sense of characterization. He achieved much of the force of his humor by the unerring consistency with which successive bits of business built up a rounded and believable character."  
>   
>  - **Cecil Smith, _Musical Comedy in America_**(New York: Theatre Arts Books, 1950), p. 93.

### Forgotten Hits
Although the versatile Wilson played many roles over the course of his long stage career, he periodically reappeared in _Erminie_, starring in a Broadway revival as late as the 1930s. Wilson was so admired by his fellow stage actors that they made him the first president of their union, Actor's Equity.
In the final years of the 19th Century, other writers and performers would bring Broadway's musical comedies a new sense of vitality.
